# Cardiovascular drug poisoning

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Cardiology and angiology > Relevant pharmacology > Cardiovascular drug poisoning*

[Original Article Link](/library/JF0sQ3)

---

## Summary

Cardiovascular drug <u>poisoning</u> can occur as a result of attempted self-harm, inadvertent <u>medication error</u>, or changes in <u>drug clearance</u>, e.g., if <u>renal insufficiency</u> develops. <u>Hypotension</u>, <u>arrhythmias</u>, and/or neurologic changes commonly occur at toxic levels of these medications. Management often requires a <u>clinical diagnosis</u> to be made based on medication history and <u>ECG</u> changes, and the patient is treated symptomatically until the offending agent is identified. Initial symptomatic treatment may include <u>GI decontamination</u>, <u>IV fluids</u> for <u>hypotension</u>, <u>atropine</u> for <u>bradycardia</u>, and <u>benzodiazepines</u> for <u>seizures</u>. Definitive therapy may include a drug class-specific <u>antidote</u>, e.g., <u>high-dose euglycemic insulin therapy</u> for <u>calcium channel blocker poisoning</u> or <u>digoxin immune Fab</u> (<u>DigiFab</u>) for <u>digoxin poisoning</u>.

---

## Clinical features

Nonspecific features common to most cases of cardiovascular drug <u>poisoning</u> include: [[2]](/library/AN1Rdh0)




* Cardiovascular features

* <u>Hypotension</u>

* <u>Bradycardia</u>

* <u>Heart blocks</u>

* <u>Reflex tachycardia</u>

* <u>Tachyarrhythmias</u>

* <u>Sudden cardiac death</u>

* Neurologic features

* <u>Somnolence</u>

* Unconsciousness

* <u>Seizures</u>

* Other features: <u>nausea and vomiting</u>





> [!WARNING]
> Patients with severe cardiovascular drug <u>poisoning</u> can present with <u>cardiogenic shock</u> or <u>cardiac arrest</u>.

---

## Beta blocker poisoning

### Potentially toxic doses [[7]](/library/soWtWm0)




Discuss risk with poison control; the lowest reported toxic dose is typically higher than the maximum recommended therapeutic dose but can overlap in drugs with a <u>narrow therapeutic index</u>.




| <br>Maximum recommended single therapeutic oral doses for common <u>beta blockers</u>  [[7]](/library/soWtWm0)<br> |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
|  | Adults | Children |
| <u>Atenolol</u> | <br>200 mg <br> | 2 mg/kg |
| <u>Carvedilol</u> | <br>50 mg <br> | 0.5 mg/kg |
| <u>Metoprolol</u> | <br>450 mg <br> | 2.5 mg/kg |
| <u>Propranolol</u> | <br>240 mg <br> | 4 mg/kg |
| <u>Sotalol</u> | <br>160 mg <br> | 4 mg/kg |
| <u>Acebutolol</u> | <br>600 mg <br> | 12 mg/kg |
| <u>Bisoprolol</u> | <br>10 mg [[29]](/library/OzaIGM)<br> | <br>0.14 mg/kg [[30]](/library/gKWFfm0)<br> |





> [!WARNING]
> <u>Bisoprolol</u> toxicity may not follow a clear <u>dose-response relationship</u>. Similar toxic effects have been seen at low and high doses of exposure. [[31]](/library/UKWbfm0)




> [!WARNING]
> A few drops of ophthalmic <u>beta blockers</u> (e.g., <u>timolol</u>) can cause significant systemic effects. [[32]](/library/66WjNm0)




### Clinical features [[2]](/library/AN1Rdh0)[[5]](/library/Y11n2f0)[[27]](/library/UTWbJk0)




#### Onset




* Life-threatening symptoms: possible as early as 30 minutes after ingestion [[5]](/library/Y11n2f0)

* Most symptoms: within the first 6 hours [[5]](/library/Y11n2f0)

* <u>Sotalol</u> <u>poisoning</u>: can cause delayed and prolonged symptoms





#### Signs and symptoms




* <u>Clinical features of CV drug poisoning</u>: typically <u>bradycardia</u>, <u>hypotension</u>, and <u>CNS depression</u>

* Other features

* <u>Delirium</u>

* Respiratory <u>depression</u>

* <u>Seizures</u> (typically seen with <u>propranolol</u>)  [[31]](/library/UKWbfm0)

* <u>Bronchospasm</u> (rare)

* <u>Adverse effects of beta blockers</u>

* <u>Clinical features of hyperkalemia</u>

* <u>Clinical features of hypoglycemia</u>





> [!TIP]
> <u>Sotalol</u> <u>poisoning</u> can manifest with <u>CNS depression</u> and <u>vomiting</u>. [[31]](/library/UKWbfm0)




### Diagnostics [[2]](/library/AN1Rdh0)[[5]](/library/Y11n2f0)[[27]](/library/UTWbJk0)




* <u>Laboratory studies</u>

* <u>BMP</u>: <u>hypoglycemia</u>, <u>hyperkalemia</u>

* <u>Blood gas</u>: <u>metabolic acidosis</u>

* Drug levels: test not generally available

* <u>ECG</u>

* <u>Sinus bradycardia</u>

* <u>AV block</u>

* Junctional <u>bradycardia</u>

* Prolonged QRS

* Additional studies

* <u>CXR</u> if the patient is at risk of <u>congestive heart failure</u>

* <u>Digoxin</u> levels if the patient is known to have had access to <u>digoxin</u>

* Additional <u>bradycardia workup</u> based on clinical suspicion





### Management [[2]](/library/AN1Rdh0)[[14]](/library/CLWq-N0)[[16]](/library/ntY7VI)[[27]](/library/UTWbJk0)[[33]](/library/HCYKtr)




If the patient is unstable, begin interventions simultaneously rather than sequentially.




#### Initial management




* Begin <u>initial management of CV drug poisoning</u>.

* <u>Hypotension</u>: IV fluid bolus 20–40 mL/kg

* <u>Symptomatic bradycardia</u>: <u>atropine</u> DOSAGE, <u>temporary cardiac pacing</u>

* <u>Sodium bicarbonate</u> (<u>off label</u>) DOSAGE if all of the following are present: [[2]](/library/AN1Rdh0)

* <u>Poisoning</u> with a membrane-stabilizing agent: e.g., <u>propranolol</u>, <u>pindolol</u>, <u>labetalol</u>, <u>oxprenolol</u>, <u>acebutolol</u>

* Acute QRS prolongation > 120 ms

* Clinical <u>signs of shock</u>





#### Persistent instability after initial management




* <u>High-dose glucagon</u> therapy

* <u>Calcium for drug poisoning</u>; may be unsafe if there is concurrent <u>digoxin poisoning</u>  [[5]](/library/Y11n2f0)[[19]](/library/XNW9-l0)[[20]](/library/BLWz-N0)

* <u>High-dose euglycemic insulin therapy</u>





> [!TIP]
> <u>Glucagon</u> can be used as an <u>antidote</u> for <u>beta blocker poisoning</u>. [[2]](/library/AN1Rdh0)[[5]](/library/Y11n2f0)




#### Sustained instability after secondary interventions




* <u>Norepinephrine infusion</u> (first line)

* <u>Vasopressin infusion</u>

* Additional <u>inotrope</u> or <u>vasopressor</u>, e.g., <u>epinephrine infusion</u> for decreased contractility





#### Refractory instability




* <u>Intravenous lipid emulsion therapy</u>

* Consider <u>hemodialysis</u> for <u>atenolol</u> or <u>sotalol</u> <u>poisoning</u> in patients with renal impairment AND refractory <u>bradycardia</u>, <u>hypotension</u>, or <u>torsades de pointes</u>.  [[34]](/library/SKWyfm0)

* <u>VA-ECMO</u>

## Digoxin poisoning

<u>Poisoning</u> may result from acute <u>digoxin overdose</u>, reduced clearance of chronically administered <u>digoxin</u>, or ingestion of plants containing <u>cardiac glycosides</u>.




### <u>Risk factors</u> [[2]](/library/AN1Rdh0)[[5]](/library/Y11n2f0)




* <u>Electrolyte</u> imbalances

* <u>Hypokalemia</u>: <u>digoxin</u> competes with <u>K<sup>+</sup></u> for binding to <u>Na<sup>+</sup>/K<sup>+</sup>-ATPase</u>

* Others: <u>hyperkalemia</u>, <u>hypernatremia</u>, <u>hypomagnesemia</u>, <u>hypercalcemia</u>, <u>alkalosis</u>

* Medical conditions

* <u>Renal failure</u> (reduced <u>digoxin</u> excretion)

* <u>Volume depletion</u> (e.g., treatment with <u>diuretics</u>)

* <u>Hypothyroidism</u>

* <u>Drug interactions</u>

* Treatment with <u>verapamil</u>, <u>diltiazem</u>, <u>amiodarone</u>, and/or <u>quinidine</u>: These drugs may displace <u>digoxin</u> from tissue binding sites and decrease <u>renal elimination</u>.

* Co-ingestion with other cardiovascular drugs (e.g., <u>beta blockers</u>) or <u>sympathomimetic drugs</u> (e.g., <u>cocaine</u>)





> [!WARNING]
> <u>Digoxin</u> has a <u>narrow therapeutic index</u>. Serum concentrations of <u>cardiac glycosides</u> must be monitored closely because overdoses can have severe consequences.




### Clinical features [[2]](/library/AN1Rdh0)[[5]](/library/Y11n2f0)[[8]](/library/bgWHFk0)[[39]](/library/O3WIiO0)




The symptoms and signs of chronic <u>digoxin poisoning</u> are nonspecific, with significant overlap between acute and chronic toxicity.




* Acute <u>poisoning</u>: Nonspecific <u>clinical features of CV drug poisoning</u> can occur.

* Acute and chronic <u>poisoning</u>: Symptoms are less obvious in chronic <u>poisoning</u>.

* <u>Vagal</u> symptoms: <u>nausea</u>, <u>vomiting</u>, <u>diarrhea</u>, abdominal <u>pain</u>, <u>anorexia</u>

* <u>Arrhythmia symptoms</u>: <u>palpitations</u>, <u>syncope</u>, and <u>presyncope</u>

* Chronic <u>poisoning</u>

* Confusion, fatigue, <u>lethargy</u>, <u>weakness</u>, and <u>disorientation</u>

* Visual disturbances

* Blurred <u>vision</u>, halos, <u>scotomas</u>, <u>diplopia</u>

* <u>Photophobia</u>

* Xanthopsia (yellow-tinted <u>vision</u>)





> [!WARNING]
> Potentially fatal <u>bradyarrhythmias</u> and/or <u>tachyarrhythmias</u> may occur in <u>digoxin poisoning</u>.




### Diagnostics [[2]](/library/AN1Rdh0)[[5]](/library/Y11n2f0)




#### <u>ECG</u> [[40]](/library/S3Wy3O0)




Any <u>dysrhythmia</u> or conduction block may occur; <u>bradyarrhythmias</u> are as common as <u>tachyarrhythmias</u>.




* <u>Premature ventricular beats</u> (most common)

* Reentry or enhanced <u>automaticity</u>: <u>Vtach</u> or <u>Vfib</u>, <u>atrial tachycardia</u> with <u>AV block</u>, <u>Afib</u> or <u>atrial flutter</u>

* Depressed conduction (<u>vagal</u> effect): <u>sinoatrial arrest</u>, <u>sinoatrial block</u>, <u>AV block</u>

* Digitalis effect: waveform changes that occur in the presence of <u>digoxin</u> but do not necessarily indicate <u>digoxin toxicity</u>  [[5]](/library/Y11n2f0)[[19]](/library/XNW9-l0)[[41]](/library/KmWUgN0)

* <u>T-wave</u> <u>inversion</u> or flattening

* Deformed <u>ST segment</u>: scooping or sagging

* ↓ <u>QT interval</u>

* ↑ <u>PR interval</u>





> [!TIP]
> There is no characteristic <u>arrhythmia</u> associated with <u>digoxin poisoning</u>; a wide range of <u>arrhythmias</u> can occur. [[2]](/library/AN1Rdh0)

#### <u>Laboratory studies</u> [[42]](/library/m3WVQO0)




* Serum <u>digoxin</u> concentration: Measure 6 hours after ingestion to avoid overtreatment unless the patient is severely symptomatic.  [[2]](/library/AN1Rdh0)[[5]](/library/Y11n2f0)[[42]](/library/m3WVQO0)

* 0.7–1.1 ng/mL: therapeutic range  [[2]](/library/AN1Rdh0)[[5]](/library/Y11n2f0)

* 1.1–3 ng/mL: indeterminate range; <u>arrhythmias</u> possible

* â¥ 2.5 ng/mL: <u>incidence</u> of <u>arrhythmia</u> > 50%

* Serum <u>electrolytes</u>

* <u>Potassium</u>: <u>hyperkalemia</u> (associated with poor prognosis)

* <u>Creatinine</u> and <u>blood urea nitrogen</u> to evaluate renal function

* Other abnormalities that may have triggered <u>digoxin poisoning</u>: See “<u>Risk factors</u>.”





### Management [[2]](/library/AN1Rdh0)[[5]](/library/Y11n2f0)[[40]](/library/S3Wy3O0)[[43]](/library/M3WMQO0)[[44]](/library/8oWOdm0)




<u>DigiFab</u> is the <u>antidote</u> for significant acute and chronic <u>poisoning</u>. [[2]](/library/AN1Rdh0)[[44]](/library/8oWOdm0)




* Initial management

* Begin <u>initial management of CV drug poisoning</u>.

* Administer <u>activated charcoal</u> even if ingestion was not recent.  [[45]](/library/ALWRZm0)

* Administer <u>digoxin immune Fab</u> (<u>DigiFab</u>), if indicated.

* <u>Electrolyte</u> abnormalities

* Treat <u>hyperkalemia</u> > 5 mEq/L with <u>DigiFab</u>; <u>calcium</u> may be unsafe.  [[5]](/library/Y11n2f0)[[19]](/library/XNW9-l0)[[20]](/library/BLWz-N0)

* Correct <u>hypokalemia</u> slowly: <u>K<sup>+</sup></u> levels may rise rapidly hours after <u>digoxin</u> ingestion. [[2]](/library/AN1Rdh0)

* Correct <u>magnesium</u> level cautiously.  [[2]](/library/AN1Rdh0)

* <u>Arrhythmia</u> treatment

* <u>DigiFab</u> therapy is preferred over pacing or <u>antiarrhythmic drugs</u>. [[2]](/library/AN1Rdh0)

* Supraventricular <u>bradyarrhythmias</u> and/or <u>high-degree AV block</u> : <u>atropine</u> DOSAGE, consider <u>temporary cardiac pacing</u>  [[40]](/library/S3Wy3O0)

* <u>ECG changes in hyperkalemia</u> : <u>sodium bicarbonate</u> (<u>off-label</u>) DOSAGE

* <u>Ventricular arrhythmias</u> or irritability

* <u>Phenytoin</u> (preferred; <u>off-label</u>) DOSAGE [[2]](/library/AN1Rdh0)[[5]](/library/Y11n2f0)

* If <u>phenytoin</u> is contraindicated or maximum <u>phenytoin</u> dose has been reached: <u>lidocaine</u> DOSAGE [[2]](/library/AN1Rdh0)[[5]](/library/Y11n2f0)





> [!WARNING]
> In severe <u>digoxin poisoning</u>, interventions such as cardiac pacing or <u>cardioversion</u> can trigger <u>asystole</u> or <u>Vfib</u>, as cardiac tissue may be hypersensitive to electrical and/or mechanical stimulation. [[2]](/library/AN1Rdh0)




> [!WARNING]
> Avoid <u>class IA antiarrhythmics</u>, e.g., <u>quinidine</u>, <u>procainamide</u>, and <u>disopyramide</u>. [[5]](/library/Y11n2f0)




### Digoxin immune Fab (<u>DigiFab</u>) [[2]](/library/AN1Rdh0)[[5]](/library/Y11n2f0)[[43]](/library/M3WMQO0)




* Fragments of <u>immunoglobulins</u> with a <u>Fab region</u> that binds free <u>digoxin</u> in the serum  [[46]](/library/qmWCgN0)

* The definitive treatment for <u>digoxin poisoning</u>





#### Indications [[2]](/library/AN1Rdh0)[[5]](/library/Y11n2f0)[[43]](/library/M3WMQO0)




Known or suspected <u>digoxin poisoning</u> in patients with any of the following:




* <u>Cardiac arrest</u> [[5]](/library/Y11n2f0)

* Any life-threatening or potentially life-threatening <u>arrhythmia</u>  [[5]](/library/Y11n2f0)

* Serum <u>potassium</u> rapidly rising or > 5 mEq/L (attributable to <u>digoxin</u>) [[2]](/library/AN1Rdh0)

* Acute ingestion > 4 mg (or > 0.1 mg/kg) in a healthy child or 10 mg in a healthy adult  [[5]](/library/Y11n2f0)

* Serum <u>digoxin</u> concentrations > 10 ng/mL soon after acute ingestion or > 6 ng/mL <u>steady state</u> [[2]](/library/AN1Rdh0)[[5]](/library/Y11n2f0)

* Serum <u>digoxin</u> concentration > 1.6 ng/mL AND signs or symptoms of severe <u>digoxin toxicity</u> [[43]](/library/M3WMQO0)

* Co-ingestion of other cardiovascular drugs





> [!TIP]
> There are no <u>absolute contraindications</u> to <u>DigiFab</u>. [[46]](/library/qmWCgN0)




#### Dosage and administration [[46]](/library/qmWCgN0)




Several strategies can be used to determine the initial dose of <u>DigiFab</u>. Expect a clinical response in most patients within 1 hour of infusion completion. [[5]](/library/Y11n2f0)




* Unknown ingested quantity: empiric administration

* Acute ingestion DOSAGE

* Chronic ingestion DOSAGE

* Known ingested quantity: ingested <u>digoxin</u> in mg x 2 = vials of <u>DigiFab</u>  [[2]](/library/AN1Rdh0)[[5]](/library/Y11n2f0)[[46]](/library/qmWCgN0)

* Known serum <u>digoxin</u> concentration: (concentration in ng/mL x patient weight in kg)/100 = vials of <u>DigiFab</u>





> [!WARNING]
> Adverse effects of Digifab include <u>hypokalemia</u>, loss of therapeutic effects of <u>digoxin</u> (e.g., rebound <u>rapid A-fib</u>), and occasionally, <u>allergic reactions</u>. [[46]](/library/qmWCgN0)




> [!WARNING]
> Monitor for recurrence of toxicity; repeat dosing of <u>DigiFab</u> is occasionally required. [[2]](/library/AN1Rdh0)
